title: Discrete outcomes with discrete predictor
text:
Discrete outcomes are everywhere. Animals are either alive or dead, plants are eaten or not, some things are just black and white.
When comparing discrete outcomes between discrete treatments, we analyze this data with lnOR or lnRR effect sizes. These effect sizes require either discrete numbers per treatment group and outcome group or proportions and group size per treatment group. If the predictor is continuous we can analyze discrete outcomes with Zr effect sizes.

title: Discrete outcomes with discrete predictor
section: Proportion or % data with total population
text:
Proportion or % data with total population








These are also straightforward. Extract the percent and reconstruct the number of individuals in each outcome category based on total n, which the authors hopefully reported in the text.

title: Discrete outcomes with discrete predictor
text:
No control group
Some experiments only report the experimental treatment, assuming that the control has a probability of 50%. In these cases, you’ll have to assume the same to calculate lnOR, e.g., by populating one of the columns with 50 / 50 values (generally with the same total N as the first row). For example, if a study only reports:

Aggregating multiple measurements
Some studies may report a response like survivorship over multiple years before and after some intervention (e.g., eradication of a predator, change in management policy, etc). The best approach is to summarize across years per treatment.

However, what do you do if there is no sample size provided (e.g., total number of individuals)? In this case, your best bet is to summarize the proportion survived into the mean ± SD across years per treatment group and use this to calculate SMD. Since these values are proportions, be sure to transform these values (see here.
Unfortunately, the resulting effect size will have year as the unit of replication instead of number of individuals and should not be directly compared to other lnOR type data where individuals are the unit of repliation.

title: Discrete outcomes with discrete predictor
text:
Mean±error discrete outcomes
Sometimes discrete outcomes are summarized into mean±error across trials/sites/islands/etc. For example, a paper that monitored fledgling rates across nests on separate islands, calculated the mortality rate, and then summarized by mean±error across islands.
This data format lends itself naturally to SMD/lnRoM/Zmu type effect sizes. However, the sample size for the mean±error in these summaries are the number of trials/sites/islands/etc instead of the number of individuals (or nests). If the unit of replication of the rest of your dataset is the number of individuals (or nests) then this effect size would have vastly less weight in your models (and should be analyzed separately).








Moreover, as you can see, this figure presents standard error, not standard deviation. Converting standard error to standard deviation requires the sample size used by the study authors to calculate standard error in the first place, which is the number of trials/sites/islands/etc.
To reconstruct the number of individuals and calculate an lnOR type effect size with individuals as the unit of replication, you can simulate the underlying binomial or beta-binomial distribution behind these mean±sd summaries. This requires the following information:

the number of sites used in calculating the standard error.
the number of individuals across all sites.
The author-reported mean proportion
The author-reported standard deviation

Let’s work through this example and imagine that the figure above was from a paper that reported nest fledging rates for 10 islands in an experimental treatment (rats poisoned) and for 10 sites in a control treatment (rats left alone). The total number of nests monitored per treatment was 300—or 30 per site. We start by converting the extracted standard error (\(se\)) to standard deviation (\(sd\)) in our data.table we extracted from the figure above:






Warning



Note that reconstructing underlying data is an experimental method. Use carefully.

Now we check whether the author-reported standard deviation is overdispersed relative to the theoretical standard deviation (\(sd_{theoretical}\)) of the binomial distribution. If it is greater than \(sd_{theoretical}\), we’ll use the beta-binomial distribution. If it isn’t, we’ll use the binomial distribution:

sd_theoretical <- sqrt((dt$mean * (1 - dt$mean))/(dt$n_individuals))

any(dt$sd > sd_theoretical)

[1] TRUE


It looks like our data is not truly binomial but beta-binomial. See here and here for how to draw from the binomial distribution.
For each our row of our extracted data (which is only 2), we will draw from the beta-binomial distribution with the R package extraDistr (Wolodzko 2023). This requires the variance (\(Var = sd^2\)) and two shape parameters that describe the beta distribution: \(\alpha\) (“alpha”) and \(\beta\) (“beta”). See here for the formulas for calculating \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\). We’ll add these to each row of the dataset dt after calculating an intermediate variable r:

library("extraDistr")
dt

dt[, var := sd^2]
dt[, r := (mean * (1 - mean) / var) - 1]
dt[, alpha := mean * r]
dt[, beta := (1 - mean) * r]

Now, we’ll draw from the beta-binomial distribution. Each draw returns a vector equal in length to the number of sites, with each element giving the number of fledged nests:

rbbinom(n = dt$n_sites[1],
        size = dt$n_individuals[1],
        alpha = dt$alpha[1], 
        beta = dt$beta[1])

 [1] 19  0  1  0  3  5 14  6  0  1


The sum of this is the total number of nests that fledged across all sites. The full workflow:

n <- c()

for(i in 1:nrow(dt)){
  n <- rbbinom(n = dt$n_sites[i],
                     size = dt$n_individuals[i],
                     alpha = dt$alpha[i], 
                     beta = dt$beta[i])
  dt[i, n_fledged := sum(n)]
}

# Now calculate total number individuals:
dt[, total_individuals := 30 * n_sites]
dt[, n_dead := total_individuals - n_fledged]

title: Discrete outcomes with discrete predictor
text:
LC50?
Many laboratory studies, for example on the effects of a pollution agent on mortality, report LC50, which is the dosage at which 50% of the exposed individuals experience an outcome (e.g., die).
These figures look like this:

#' @Kyle?

LC50 is already its own formula. We do not know how to convert this to lnOR or lnRR. If you’re faced with lots of this data, you could consider converting survivorship curves, or other data sources, to LC50—and deriving a sampling variance formula or using SAFE to simulate sampling variance.
It is possible that you can calculate single-group proportion effect sizes (especially probit transformed proportions) to describe data like this, but your results may be difficult to compare to other effect sizes in your dataset

title: Effect sizes in meta-analysis
text:
Introduction
Meta-analysis has grown to be one of the powerful methods in science. By extracting data from across the literature, a meta-analyst can answer age-old questions at scales previously unimaginable. Moreover, meta-analysis can test for and correct publication bias and can thus not only control for biases in the literature base but provide a bridge between empirical questions (i.e., what is) and metascientific questions (e.g., how scientists construct knowledge).
Meta-analysis can be really hard. Meta-analytic methods continue to proliferate, with new effect sizes, models, and methods being published constantly. The literature has become a minefield of articles and tutorials of ‘best practices’ that can be bewildering for even the most experienced meta-analyst to keep up with.
We here present a living tutorial to navigating this methodological tempest, with particular emphasis on understanding effect sizes and extracting them from a variety of data formats. This tutorial is maintained by the Collaboration for Open Science and Synthesis in Ecology and Evolution at the University of Alberta, which is led by Professor Shinichi Nakagawa—one of the principle developers of new meta-analytic methods. While many of the examples in this tutorial derive from our experiences in ecology and evolution, which is rife with messy data, we believe the contents are applicable broadly.
We hope that this tutorial, by integrating tips and tricks and statistical know-how from across the decades and into the future, can increase the consistency, reliability, and reproducibility of meta-analytic research.
Should we add more of an overview of what meta-analysis is?


How to use this tutorial
We begin by discussing the dominant effect size types, their numeric assumptions, and how to interpret them. We then discuss the nuts and bolts of planning data extraction.
We then go into detail about universal challenges in extracting and calculating effect sizes and present effect-size specific pages about how to deal with the many odd and unusual data formats that you may uncover.
We conclude with a discussion of how to convert between effect size types. Finally, we also present some additional helpful material, including descriptions of effect sizes that estimate differences in variability and magnitude between groups and effect sizes for single group descriptive statistics. These effect size types are also summarized in a cheatsheet for the many options available in metafor’s escalc function (Viechtbauer 2010)—the workhorse of effect size calculation and meta-analysis.
This tutorial is based on an R workflow and assumes that the users have a basic understanding of R. This tutorial is viewable as a webpage or you can clone the repo and run the .qmd files interactively.


Voyaging among the ghosts of data past
Meta-analyses are powerful. But they are full of tedium. And dealing with the challenges that we describe in this tutorial (hopefully in plain english) can be overwhelming.
Yet there is something beautiful and very human about doing a meta-analysis. You encounter the heartwork and hardwork of dozens or hundreds or thousands of fellow human beings. Stories from last year or 50 years ago, from people exploring, observing, experimenting, and trying to understand our universe.
These voyagers left us breadcrumbs. Sometimes as simple as a mean and a standard deviation. Sometimes as complex as some strange contour plot drawn on a piece of graph paper and scanned in 1975. Extracting their data summaries (or finding their raw datasets) brings their work to life and allows us to continue their quests.
While you struggle to deal with all the strange and bizarre and difficult and annoying decisions these voyagers sometimes made to communicate their tales, remember to feel compassion and awe for the work that came before us–these efforts to describe the mysteries of our world.


A living tutorial
This tutorial is a living document. As such, please help us keep it alive and useful. If we missed anything, if we made an error, or overlooked an extraction challenge, please file an Issue on our github page here.







References

Viechtbauer, W. 2010. Conducting meta-analyses in R with the metafor package. Journal of Statistical Software 36:1–48.

title: An overview of effect sizes
text:
Alternative estimators
You’ll also notice, for example if looking at the documentation of escalc, that there are many many effect size estimators that are similar to the primary effect size flavors covered here yet have small differences that can be difficult to disentangle. These are often rarely used despite their potential utility to meta-analyses.
Some of these estimates can be lumped with the typical effect size flavors. Others cannot.
One of the most statistically important alternative flavors account for paired designs—i.e., non-independence between control and experimental groups. For example, before-after data or paired plot comparisons. These are common experimental designs in ecology and evolution but most meta-analyses do not take into account for this non-independence.
Some paired-design formulas produce effect sizes and sampling variance estimates that are comparable to those produced from unpaired formulas. In these cases, the effect size point estimate will be the same, or nearly the same, regardless of the paired/unpaired formulation. However, the sampling variance for the paired design will be lower—which will give paired design data more weight in downstream meta-analytic models.
We try to clear up this confusion in the appendix with some charts of compatibility between the different estimators in escalc.

title: Differences in magnitude between two groups
text:
The effect sizes that we’ve described in depth in this tutorial have concerned either mean relationships or differences in variability. However, what if you’re interested in the magnitude of mean differences, regardless of their direction? These types of questions are common in evolution, where absolute differences between two populations are of interest but directionality of those differences is inconsequential. Likewise, some ecological moderators (like population density) may influence magnitude of ecological effects but not their directionality.
Previous attempts to conduct meta-analyses of magnitude have used the absolute value of SMD as an effect size (or ‘folded-normal SMD’). However, taking the absolute value of SMD produces effect sizes clustered just above 0 with distributions that violate expectations of normality and can prevent accurate model estimates.
lnM is a recently developed effect size that is unbounded and normally distributed and describes the absolute difference between two groups (Nakagawa et al. 2026a).
To calculate lnM, you need the same statistical ingredients as for calculating SMD and lnRoM effect sizes: sample sizes (\(n_1\), \(n_2\)), means (\(m_1\), \(m_2\)), and standard deviations (\(sd_1\), \(sd_2\)) for two discrete groups.
The math for lnM is built upon classical one-way ANOVA building blocks. Because the math is a bit long, we’ve hidden it in the folded block below. Click to see.






Noteclick here to see the mathematics of lnM





lnM is based on the classical ANOVA building blocks. First we calculate Mean Square Between (\(MS_B\)) and Mean Square Within (\(MS_W\)). \(MS_B\) estimates the difference between group means. \(MS_W\) estimates the variance inside of each group.
\[
\begin{aligned}
&MS_B = \frac{n_1 n_2}{n_1 + n_2} * (m_1 - m_2)^2\\
&MS_W = \frac{(n_1 - 1)sd_1^2 + (n_2 - 1)sd_2^2}{n_1 + n_2 - 2}\\
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}\]
We then establish within-group (\(s_W^2\)) and between-group variance (\(s_B^2\)), standardized by harmonic-mean sample size (\(n_0\)).
\[
\begin{aligned}
&n_0 = \frac{2n_1n_2}{n_1 + n_2}\\
&s_W^2 = MS_W\\
&s_B^2 = \frac{MS_B - MS_W}{n_0} \\
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}\]
Finally, with use these ingredients to calculate lnM as the ratio of between group standard deviation (\(s_B\)) and within-group standard deviation (\(s_W\)):
\[
\begin{aligned}
&lnM = \ln\left(\frac{s_B}{s_W}\right)\\
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}\]



How to calculate lnM
If the means of group 1 and group 2 are similar, lnM cannot be calculated algebraically because of 0’s in the denominator. For this reason, lnM should be estimated with SAFE bootstrapping (Nakagawa et al. 2026b), which simulates hyperparameters based on summary statistics (i.e., \(m_{1,2}\), \(sd_{1,2}\)) and thus, if repeated enough, can produce estimates of lnM.
As such, lnM is not currently supported by metafor::escalc and has to be calculated in metatools::eff_size.
Be sure to set SAFE=TRUE in the function arguments. The SAFE_boots argument indicates how many bootstraps to run (1e6 is default and appears to be a good compromise between accuracy and speed). SAFE_max_secs is the number of seconds to run before timing out per effect size calculation. Calculating lnM can be time consuming because calculations must be done over and over until a sufficient number of bootstraps is attained.
Let’s create a dataset with 2 row for which we want to calculate lnM. Note that the first row of this data has means that are very similar (15 and 15.5) between the two groups and will thus require more time to run:

if(!requireNamespace("metatools")) {
  pak::pak("ejlundgren/metatools")
}
library("metatools")


dat <- data.table(x1 = c(15, 15), x2 = c(15.5, 20),
                  sd1 = c(2, 2), sd2 = c(2, 2),
                  n1 = c(15, 15), n2 = c(15, 15))

yi in the resulting table is the algebraic point estimate. You’ll note that yi for the first row is NA. This is because the difference between x1 and x2 is very small, leading to incalculable values.
SAFE circumvents this by bootstrapping from the means and standard deviations until a sufficient number of bootstraps is reached (defined by SAFE_boots, here set to 1e6). The point estimate and sampling variance produced by SAFE bootstrapping are reported as yi_safe and vi_safe. Additional information on the performance of the SAFE boostrapping are returned as well (number_SAFE_iterations, number_SAFE_bootstraps_completed, SAFE_elapsed_time, SAFE_complete). See function documentation for more information (?eff_size).






Note



Cases where the means between groups are very similar may take a while to successfully run. Increase SAFE_max_secs and reduce SAFE_boots until your dataset produces finalized SAFE estimates, indicated by the SAFE_complete column. We recommend not reducing SAFE_boots less than 1e4 (1e5 and 1e6 are preferable).
To learn more about SAFE see the tutorial here and Nakagawa et al. (2026b).

Interpretation
lnM is the ratio of between group variation and within-group variation. This between group standard deviation can be thought of as mean-separation—how far apart the two groups are.
However, lnM can be difficult to interpret. An lnM of 0 corresponds to identical between and within group variation. This should not be interpreted as equal group means but whether the between-group dispersion is at least as large as the within-group dispersion.
While meta-analytic models should be fit on lnM directly, we recommend mapping lnM model estimates and confidence intervals to SMD, or \(d\), for interpretation. We’ll refer to this as \(d_{eq}\) (“d-equivalent”):
\[
\begin{aligned}
&n_0 = \frac{2 n_1 n_2}{n_1 + n_2}\\
&d_{eq} = \sqrt{2e^{2lnM} + \frac{2}{n_0}}\\
\end{aligned}
\tag{4}\]
Note that when lnM = 0, this translates to \(d_{eq}\) of 1.41. What exactly does that mean? This means that within-group variation is large but overall mean differences between groups are 1.41 standard deviations apart. Tricky right?
However, what would you provide for \(n_0\) if you want to convert model estimates and confidence intervals to \(d_{eq}\)? Luckily, Nakagawa et al. (2026a) provided a large-sample approximation for \(d_{eq}\) that does not require \(n_0\). This is defined as:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&d_{eq} \approx \sqrt{2} \times e^{lnM}
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}\]
Use this equation to convert model estimates and CIs to \(d_{eq}\).
Let’s illustrate lnM in R for three comparisons—each representing a plausible comparison of group 1 and 2. We’ll draw data from the normal distribution for 3 scenarios: equivalent “true” means, and increasing means for group 2. We’ll set the group standard deviations constant at 5, and change the means of group 2 by increments of 5 while holding group 1 constant at \(m_1=15\). In order to clearly illustrate how lnM works, we’ll set a sample size of 500 for each group—which would be an unusually high sample size for a meta-analytic dataset. We’ll plot the simulated data, lnM estimates, and \(d_{eq}\). We’ll calculate \(d_{eq}\) using Equation 4 because sample size is known (since these are point estimates and not model estimates).

Codeset.seed(7)

# 
sd <- 5
n <- 500

# Group 1 distribution (fixed):
group_1 <- rnorm(n = n, mean = 15, sd = sd)

# Group 2 distributions:
distributions <- lapply(c(15, 20, 25),
                        function(x) data.table(mean_group_2 = x,
                                               group_2 = rnorm(n = n, mean = x, sd = sd))) |>
  rbindlist()

distributions[, group_1 := rep(group_1, length(unique(distributions$mean)))]

dat_summaries <- distributions[, .(x1 = mean(group_1),
                                   x2 = mean(group_2),
                                   sd1 = sd(group_1),
                                   sd2 = sd(group_2),
                                   n1 = 40,
                                   n2 = 40),
                               by = .(mean_group_2)]
dat_summaries

dat_summaries <- eff_size(x1 = x1, x2 = x2, 
                           sd1 = sd1, sd2 = sd2,
                           n1 = n1, n2 = n2,
                           data = dat_summaries,
                           bind = TRUE,
                           effect_type = "lnM",
                           verbose = FALSE,
                           SAFE = TRUE,
                           SAFE_boots = 1e6,
                           SAFE_max_secs = 15)
dat_summaries

d_eq <- function(lnM, n1, n2){
  n0 = (2*n1*n2) / (n1 + n2)
  sqrt(2*exp(2*lnM) + (2/n0))
}

# Calculate d_eq:
dat_summaries[, deq := d_eq(lnM = yi_safe, n1 = n1, n2 = n2)]

# Create string labels:
dat_summaries[, estimates := paste0("lnM = ", round(yi_safe, 2), 
                                    ";<br>d<sub>eq</sub> = ", round(deq, 2))]
dat_summaries[, scenario := paste0("m<sub>1</sub>=", round(x1, 1), ", sd<sub>1</sub>=", round(sd1, 1),
                                   "<br>",
                                   "m<sub>2</sub>=", round(x2, 1),  ", sd<sub>2</sub>=", round(sd2, 1))]

# Format distributions to be long and have labels:
distributions.mlt <- melt(distributions,
                            id.vars = c("mean_group_2"))
distributions_final <- merge(distributions.mlt,
                             dat_summaries[, .(mean_group_2, estimates)],
                             by = "mean_group_2")
distributions_final

# Sort:
setorder(distributions_final, mean_group_2)
distributions_final$estimates <- factor(distributions_final$estimates,
                                     levels = unique(distributions_final$estimates))

setorder(dat_summaries, mean_group_2)
dat_summaries$estimates <- factor(dat_summaries$estimates,
                                     levels = unique(distributions_final$estimates))

# distributions_final[, facet_lab := paste("")]
distributions_final$variable <- factor(distributions_final$variable,
                                       c("group_1", "group_2"))

p <- ggplot()+
  geom_density(data = distributions_final, aes(x = value, fill = variable),
               alpha = 0.75)+
  geom_richtext(data = dat_summaries,
            aes(x = 20, y = 0.1, label = scenario), 
            size = 4, label.color = NA, fill = "transparent")+
  facet_wrap(~estimates)+
  ylab("Density")+
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 0.11))+
  scale_fill_manual(name = NULL,
                    labels = c("group_1" = "Group 1", "group_2" = "Group 2"),
                    values = c("group_1" = "goldenrod", "group_2" = "dodgerblue"))+
  theme_bw()+
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(),
        strip.background = element_blank(),
        strip.text = ggtext::element_markdown(size = 14),
        legend.position = "bottom")










The figure shows the the realized means and standard deviations of groups 1 and 2 (\(m_{1,2}\), \(sd_{1,2}\)) after drawing their distributions from the normal distribution.
In the first panel, the means and standard deviations of group 1 and 2 are nearly identical. Yet lnM is -1.94 and not 0. Intuitively this is confusing—you’d expect no difference! But lnM doesn’t work that way because lnM is the ratio of within to between variance. That’s where \(d_{eq}\) comes in handy: \(d_{eq} = 0.3\). This means that the two groups are ~1/3 of a standard deviation apart—a negligible difference.
In the second panel, \(m_2\) is now ~20. lnM is -0.4 and \(d_{eq}\) is ~1. This makes sense because the standard deviation is 5 and \(m_2\) is now ~5 away from \(m_1\)

This can be reported as: “There was 1 standard deviation between groups”

In the third panel, \(m_2\) is 25, lnM is 0.34 and \(d_{eq}\) is 2. This also makes sense because the \(m_2\) is now 2 standard deviations away from \(m_1\).

“There were 2 standard deviations between groups”

As you can see, converting lnM to \(d_{eq}\) makes the results intepretable in terms of differences in standard deviation between two groups—just like with SMD. However, unlike SMD, these differences are directionless. It doesn’t matter which group is higher or lower: the result will be the same.
Analyzing lnM, which is a normally distributed and unbounded effect size, allows us to ask evolutionary and ecological questions that have previously been unanswerable with meta-analysis. Converting model estimates and confidence intervals to \(d_{eq}\) (using Equation 5) allows us to report these summaries in more or less plain english (well, at least as plain as we can report SMD).





Meta-analytic models with lnM
Because of the distributional properties of lnM and \(d_{eq}\), you should fit models directly on lnM instead of on \(d_{eq}\).
However, this can lead to challenges in interpreting the statistical outputs: by default the statistical tests performed by metafor::rma.mv compare coefficients to 0: a p-value of 0.01 indicate that a coefficient is significantly different than 0.
However, for lnM, 0 does not mean the same as it does for other effect sizes: as our simulation above shows, identical means and standard deviations produce an lnM of -1.94. For this reason, we do not recommend reporting p-values for lnM meta-analyses. Instead, convert the model estimates and CIs to \(d_{eq}\) (using Equation 5) and interpret them directly.
We’ll demonstrate with a dataset provided by metafor:

data(dat.normand1999)

dat.normand1999 <- eff_size(x1 = m1i, x2 = m1i, 
                           sd1 = sd1i, sd2 = sd2i,
                           n1 = n1i, n2 = n2i,
                           data = dat.normand1999,
                           bind = TRUE,
                           effect_type = "lnM",
                           verbose = FALSE,
                           SAFE = TRUE,
                           SAFE_boots = 1e6,
                           SAFE_max_secs = 15)

At least one plugin effect size could not be calculated

m <- rma.mv(yi = yi_safe,
            V = vi_safe,
            data = dat.normand1999,
            random = ~1|study,
            method = "REML",
            test = "t")

m # Comparison to 0

sigma^2    0.0000  0.0000      9     no   study

The p value and test statistic in the model table above show strong evidence that lnM is significantly different than 0 (t = -8.8, p < 0.0001). But 0 is not particularly meaningful.
For that reason, we’ll convert the model estimates and CIs to \(d_{eq}\) and interpret those in plain english:

d_eq_approx <- function(lnM){
  sqrt(2) * exp(lnM)
}

broom.mixed::tidy(m) %>% # create a tidy table of model object
  mutate(ci.lb = m$ci.lb,
         ci.ub = m$ci.ub) %>% # Add CIs to table
  mutate(estimate_deq = d_eq_approx(estimate),
         ci.lb.deq = d_eq_approx(ci.lb),
         ci.ub.deq = d_eq_approx(ci.ub)) %>%
  select(term, estimate, ci.lb, ci.ub, estimate_deq, ci.lb.deq, ci.ub.deq) %>%
  knitr::kable()

We can then report that the magnitude of differences between groups was ~0.19 standard deviations, with 95% confidence intervals ranging from 0.11 to 0.32 standard deviations. We can use the same approximate benchmarks as we use with SMD:

\(d_{eq} \approx |0.2|\) is a weak difference
\(d_{eq} \approx |0.5|\) is a moderate difference
\(d_{eq} \approx |0.8|\) is a strong difference







Note



Alternatively, you can use the function anova to set an alternative null value than 0. This is done as follows:

anova(m, rhs = -1.5)


Test of Moderators (coefficient 1):
F(df1 = 1, df2 = 8) = 4.8652, p-val = 0.0585


This compared the model estimate to an lnM of -1.5 and returned F = 4.8, p = 0.058. However, choosing what this null value should be is non-trivial. There is no way to solve Equation 5 for \(d_eq\) of 0 (because the result is \(-\infty\)). For that reason, we don’t recommend using anova unless there is a good a priori justification for your null hypothesis value.


Assumptions
lnM works with both ratio-scale and interval-scale data and can thus accept negative values.
However, as with SMD and lnRoM, lnM assumes that the underlying data is more or less normally distributed. We recommend checking for overdispersed data and excluding effect sizes with \(CV > 2\), as with SMD and lnRoM. See here for further discussion of overdispersion. lnM is also sensitive to low sample sizes. Nakagawa et al. (2026a) recommends conducting sensitivity analyses only including studies with \(n_1 + n_2 \geq 40\).
lnM is a newly constructed effect size (as of 2026). Further research is necessary to understand how heteroscedasticity and other numeric properties influence lnM performance.
Further reading
Please see Nakagawa et al. (2026a) and the associated tutorial for more information about lnM.





References

title: Single-group effect sizes
text:
While most meta-analyses concern the relationships between two variables, often reflecting experimental treatments, sometimes we’re interested in summarizing single-group measurements and then analyzing these measurements in relation to moderators.
For example, imagine you want to understand the drivers of predator attacks on livestock. Various studies have reported predator diets or kill frequencies, allowing you to obtain the proportion of diet that contains livestock (Dhungana et al. 2026). These single-group proportions can be converted to effect sizes (so that they obtain a sampling variance estimation). You can then use metaregression to evaluate the influence of various moderators (e.g., human density, elevation, prey density) on predator depredation rates of livestock.

title: Single-group effect sizes
text:
Single group means
The single group standardized mean is the mean divided by standard deviation (\(\frac{m}{sd}\)) to create a unit-free index, similar to SMD. As such, this effect size can accept values ≤ 0.
In escalc this can be calculated with measure="SMN":

escalc(measure = "SMN",
       mi = 10,
       sdi = 1.5,
       ni = 15)

This, like SMD, can be interpreted as the number of standard deviations the mean is from 0. Given that standard deviation influences the mean, this effect size may be less preferred with overdispersed data (as with SMD). See here, where we discuss how to diagnose overdispersion in your data.

title: Single-group effect sizes
text:
Log-transformed mean
The log-transformed mean (\(\log(m)\)) is a single group corollary to lnRoM. This effect size cannot accept negative values. As with lnRoM, the point estimate for log-transformed mean is not influenced by standard deviation, which is instead accounted for by the sampling variance estimate.
In escalc:

escalc(measure = "MNLN",
       mi = 10,
       sdi = 1.5,
       ni = 15)

As such, this effect size is likely better suited for overdispersed data.
